lead: Logistic regression answers a yes/no question with a probability. It takes the linear score w·x + b from chapter 2.1, passes it through the sigmoid so the output lies between 0 and 1, and then compares that probability against a threshold to give a class. Training maximises the likelihood of the observed 0/1 labels, which produces the binary cross-entropy loss. Banks use it to score loan defaults, hospitals to flag risk, and email systems to filter spam — anywhere you want a calibrated probability and an explainable linear boundary rather than just a label.
prereq: You need: the linear score w·x + b from 2.1, gradient descent from 2.2, and basic probability from Unit 1.

sections.h3: Why a straight line cannot be a probability

blocks.text: A linear model computes z = w·x + b, a score that can be any real number. Treating that score directly as a probability fails: it can come out as 1.7 or −0.4. Fitting a line to 0/1 labels by least squares is also badly behaved, because it punishes a confidently correct prediction — a label-1 point with score 3 has squared error 4, so the fit is dragged towards the middle.

blocks.where: σ(z) is the predicted probability of class 1; z = w·x + b is the linear score; w is the weight vector; x is the feature vector; b is the bias; e ≈ 2.718 is the base of natural logarithms.

blocks.text: The sigmoid squashes any real number into the open interval (0, 1). At z = 0 it gives exactly 0.5. It rises towards 1 for large positive z and falls towards 0 for large negative z, never touching either end, so the odds stay finite. Equivalently, the log-odds are linear in x.

blocks.where: p is the probability of class 1; p/(1−p) is the odds; the left-hand side is the log-odds, also called the logit.

blocks.text: So logistic regression is linear in the log-odds, not in p. Some syllabi call it the logit model for exactly this reason. At p = 0.5 the logit is 0, which is why the score z = 0 and the 0.5 threshold line up.

sections.h3: Maximum likelihood gives the cross-entropy loss

blocks.text: Training asks which w and b make the observed labels most likely. For one example with true label y ∈ {0, 1} and predicted probability p, the model assigns probability p to label 1 and 1 − p to label 0. Both cases fit in one expression: p^y (1 − p)^(1−y).
Multiply that over all n training examples, take the natural log to turn the product into a sum, negate it, and divide by n. The result is the binary cross-entropy loss, also called log loss.
L = −(1/n) Σᵢ [ yᵢ ln pᵢ + (1 − yᵢ) ln(1 − pᵢ) ]
blocks.where: n is the number of training examples; yᵢ ∈ {0,1} is the true label of example i; pᵢ = σ(w·xᵢ + b) is its predicted probability; ln is the natural logarithm.

blocks.text: Differentiate and the gradient comes out simple: the derivative with respect to weight wⱼ is (1/n) Σᵢ (pᵢ − yᵢ) xᵢⱼ. That is average prediction error times the feature value, the same shape as the linear regression gradient. There is no closed-form solution, so we descend.

items: Initialise w and b, usually to zeros.
Compute zᵢ = w·xᵢ + b and pᵢ = σ(zᵢ) for every training example.
Compute g_w = (1/n) Σ (pᵢ − yᵢ) xᵢ and g_b = (1/n) Σ (pᵢ − yᵢ).
Update w ← w − α g_w and b ← b − α g_b, where α is the learning rate.
Repeat until the loss stops falling. This is batch gradient descent from 2.2.

sections.h3: The boundary is linear, the threshold is your choice

blocks.text: To output a label, pick a threshold t and predict class 1 when p ≥ t. The default t = 0.5 is the same as testing z ≥ 0. The set of inputs where z = 0 is the decision boundary: a straight line in two dimensions, a plane in three, a hyperplane in general. Because z is linear in x, that boundary can never curve.

The threshold is a separate decision, not part of the fitted probability. Lower it to 0.2 in a cancer screen and you catch more cases at the price of false alarms. Raise it to 0.9 in a filter that silently deletes mail, because losing a real message costs more than letting spam through. Always state which threshold was used when you report accuracy.

Being linear, logistic regression cannot wrap around a ring of one class inside another. Polynomial features or kernels (Unit 3) fix that. For K classes, replace the sigmoid with the softmax over K scores, p_k = e^(z_k)/Σ_j e^(z_j), and train with categorical cross-entropy. 2.4 studies such linear boundaries directly.

figure.caption: The sigmoid turns the score z = −5 + 2x into a probability. It crosses 0.5 at x = 2.5, the decision boundary: x = 1 gives p = 0.047 (class 0) and x = 3 gives p = 0.731 (class 1).

spec.aria: An S-shaped sigmoid curve of p against x from 0 to 5, crossing the dashed 0.5 threshold at x = 2.5. The region right of x = 2.5 is shaded as class 1. Marked points: x = 1 with p = 0.047 and x = 3 with p = 0.731.

examples.question: A logistic regression model on a single input x has linear score z = −5 + 2x. (a) Find the predicted probability at x = 3. (b) Find the decision boundary for a 0.5 threshold. (c) Find the predicted probability at x = 1 and state the predicted class at threshold 0.5.
steps: Evaluate the score at x = 3: z = −5 + 2(3) = −5 + 6 = 1.
The boundary at threshold 0.5 is where p = 0.5, which means z = 0: −5 + 2x = 0, so 2x = 5 and x = 2.5.
Evaluate the score at x = 1: z = −5 + 2(1) = −3.
Compare with the threshold: 0.047 < 0.5, so the model predicts class 0 at x = 1.
examples.answer: p = 0.731 at x = 3; the 0.5 boundary is at x = 2.5; p = 0.047 at x = 1, which gives class 0.
examples.check:
import math
def sigmoid(z):
    return 1/(1+math.exp(-z))
z3 = -5 + 2*3
print(round(sigmoid(z3), 3))
print(round(5/2, 3))
z1 = -5 + 2*1
print(round(sigmoid(z1), 3))

traps: Fitting w and b by least squares on 0/1 labels and calling the result logistic regression. That is a linear probability model: it can predict outside [0, 1] and is not maximum likelihood.
Treating p = 0.73 as the answer. The class label exists only after a threshold is fixed; the probability is the model's output, the label is your decision.
Forgetting that the threshold can move. Two teams with identical fitted weights can ship different classifiers by choosing t = 0.3 and t = 0.7.
Using log base 2 in the loss. The derivation and the neat gradient (p − y) both assume the natural logarithm, ln.

quiz.q: Write the sigmoid function and give its value at z = 0.
Why is a linear function unsuitable as a probability, and why is least squares a poor training rule here?
quiz.a: A linear function is unbounded, so it can return values below 0 or above 1. Least squares on 0/1 labels also penalises a confidently correct prediction — a label-1 point with score 3 contributes squared error 4 — so the fit is pulled towards the middle instead of becoming confident.

quiz.q: With z = −5 + 2x, find p at x = 4 to three decimals.
A model predicts p = 0.8 for an example whose true label is 1. What is this example's contribution to the binary cross-entropy loss?
quiz.a: The contribution is −ln(0.8) = 0.223. The (1 − y) term vanishes because y = 1.

quiz.q: A hospital screens for a rare disease where a missed case is dangerous and a follow-up test is cheap. Should the threshold be below, at, or above 0.5? Justify with the costs.
quiz.a: Below 0.5, for example 0.2. A false negative (missed disease) costs far more than a false positive that only triggers a follow-up test. Lowering the threshold raises recall, at the cost of lower precision; the probability model is unchanged, only the decision rule moves.

quiz.q: Show that the gradient of binary cross-entropy with respect to wⱼ is (1/n) Σ (pᵢ − yᵢ) xᵢⱼ.
quiz.a: For one example, dL/dp = −y/p + (1 − y)/(1 − p). The sigmoid derivative is dp/dz = p(1 − p). Multiplying gives −y(1 − p) + (1 − y)p = p − y. Then dz/dwⱼ = xⱼ, so dL/dwⱼ = (p − y)xⱼ. Averaging over n examples gives (1/n) Σ (pᵢ − yᵢ) xᵢⱼ.

quiz.q: Why does the 0.5 threshold correspond to the score z = 0?
quiz.a: σ(0) = 0.5 and the sigmoid is strictly increasing, so p ≥ 0.5 exactly when z ≥ 0. The boundary is therefore the set of inputs where w·x + b = 0.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry the probability matters as much as the label: credit scoring, insurance pricing and clinical risk all consume p directly, so teams check calibration with reliability diagrams and repair it with Platt scaling or isotonic regression. Logistic regression is also the final layer of most neural classifiers — a softmax over K scores — so the same loss reappears in Unit 5 under a new name. Search 'log loss derivation', 'class imbalance threshold moving' and 'Platt scaling' to go further.
